propositions.text: Ms. Dabar argues the PRRA officer unreasonably found no well-founded fear of persecution based on mental illness and gender.
propositions.quote: She argues that the PRRA officer unreasonably found that she would not have a well-founded fear of persecution based on mental illness and gender upon returning to her country of origin, Djibouti.

propositions.text: I am dismissing her application because the officer’s analysis was reasonable and based on established legal principles.
propositions.quote: I am dismissing her application, because the officer’s analysis of the evidence was reasonable and based on established legal principles.

propositions.text: Ms. Dabar seeks judicial review of the denial of her PRRA application.
propositions.quote: Ms. Dabar is seeking judicial review of the denial of her application for a pre-removal risk assessment [PRRA].

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Dabar seeks judicial review alleging unreasonable PRRA officer findings; court dismisses application as officer's analysis was reasonable.

propositions.text: Ms. Dabar is a Djibouti citizen who alleges police assaulted her and closed her store due to political opposition support.
propositions.quote: Ms. Dabar is a citizen of Djibouti. She alleges that because of her support for the Mouvement pour le renouveau démocratique et le développement [MRD], an opposition party, the police severely assaulted her and closed her store, taking away all her stock.

propositions.text: She fled to Canada and claimed refugee protection alleging political persecution fear.
propositions.quote: She eventually fled to Canada and claimed refugee protection, alleging a fear of political persecution.

propositions.text: The RPD dismissed her claim due to lack of credibility.
propositions.quote: The Refugee Protection Division [RPD] of the Immigration and Refugee Board [IRB] dismissed her claim, because it found her not to be credible.

propositions.text: Her RAD appeal was dismissed as never perfected.
propositions.quote: Her appeal to the Refugee Appeal Division [RAD] of the IRB was never perfected and was dismissed.

propositions.text: Her application to re-open the case was dismissed.
propositions.quote: Her application to re-open the case was dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Dabar alleges political persecution in Djibouti; RPD dismissed claim for credibility; RAD appeal and re-opening dismissed.

propositions.text: Ms. Dabar applied for PRRA citing risks from political opinion, ethnicity, gender, and mental illness.
propositions.quote: Ms. Dabar then applied for a PRRA. She relied on risks related to her political opinion, ethnicity, gender and mental illness.

propositions.text: PRRA officer found new evidence did not overcome RPD credibility findings on political opinion.
propositions.quote: With respect to political opinion, the PRRA officer found that the new evidence filed by Ms. Dabar did not overcome the RPD’s credibility findings.

propositions.text: Officer acknowledged discrimination against women, but noted Ms. Dabar operated a business, is married, and has family support.
propositions.quote: The officer then acknowledged the documentary evidence regarding discrimination against women in Djibouti, in particular against single women, but noted that Ms. Dabar successfully operated a business, that she is still married and that she could rely on her family’s support.

propositions.text: Officer found little evidence Ms. Dabar would be personally affected by ethnic discrimination.
propositions.quote: The officer also found that there was little evidence that Ms. Dabar would be personally affected by discrimination based on her ethnic origin.

propositions.text: Officer found PTSD origin unclear and that remote treatment could be pursued if mental health support limited in Djibouti.
propositions.quote: Lastly, with respect to mental illness, the officer found that the origin of Ms. Dabar’s post-traumatic stress disorder [PTSD] was unclear, and that she could pursue remote treatment over the Internet if mental health support in Djibouti was too limited.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Dabar applied for PRRA citing multiple risks; officer found credibility issues, acknowledged discrimination but noted mitigating factors, and unclear PTSD origin.

propositions.text: I dismiss Ms. Dabar’s application because the PRRA officer’s decision was reasonable.
propositions.quote: I am dismissing Ms. Dabar’s application, because the PRRA officer’s decision was reasonable.

propositions.text: Officer did not misapprehend evidence and provided logical analysis to reject claim.
propositions.quote: The officer did not misapprehend the evidence and provided a logical chain of analysis to justify the rejection of Ms. Dabar’s claim.

propositions.text: Some reasons could be more carefully worded but this does not affect overall reasonableness.
propositions.quote: Certain aspects of the reasons could have been more carefully worded, but this do not affect the reasonableness of the whole.

propositions.text: Judicial review is not a line-by-line error search and only intervenes if officer fundamentally misapprehended evidence.
propositions.quote: After all, judicial review is not a “line-by-line treasure hunt for error”: Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 at paragraph 102, [2019] 4 SCR 653 [Vavilov]. Neither is judicial review an opportunity to advocate for a different weighing of the evidence. The Court will intervene only if the officer “fundamentally misapprehended or failed to account for the evidence before it”: Vavilov, at paragraph 126.

paragraphs.summary: Court dismisses application, finds officer’s decision reasonable with logical analysis; cites Vavilov on judicial review limits.

propositions.text: Ms. Dabar relied mainly on psychotherapist report alleging persecution based on mental health.
propositions.quote: In her PRRA application, Ms. Dabar relied mainly on the report of a psychotherapist to allege that her return to Djibouti would expose her to persecution based on her mental health condition.

propositions.text: Psychotherapist report recounts political persecution allegations found not credible and mentions ethnic discrimination not challenged.
propositions.quote: The report recounts her allegations of persecution based on political opinion, which were found not credible by the RPD. It also mentions discrimination based on ethnicity; the PRRA officer found that this did not amount to a personalized risk of persecution and Ms. Dabar does not challenge that aspect of the decision.

propositions.text: Report states Ms. Dabar has PTSD symptoms, treatment sessions, and lack of trauma-informed services may worsen symptoms.
propositions.quote: The report then states that Ms. Dabar exhibits certain symptoms consistent with PTSD, briefly describes the treatment sessions she is undergoing and concludes by stating that “[t]he lack of support and appropriate trauma informed services may exasperate [sic] Mrs. Abdi Dabar’s symptoms mentioned above and impede her recovery.”

propositions.text: Ms. Dabar also relies on country evidence showing mental health services are largely non-existent in Djibouti.
propositions.quote: Ms. Dabar also relies on country condition evidence showing that mental health services are largely non-existent in Djibouti.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Dabar relies on psychotherapist report and country evidence alleging mental health persecution risk; political and ethnic claims not challenged.

propositions.text: Ms. Dabar argues removal to Djibouti would worsen her PTSD and lack of treatment would harm her mental health.
propositions.quote: Based on this evidence, Ms. Dabar argued that her removal to Djibouti would exacerbate her condition, because this is where the abuse that caused her PTSD occurred. She also alleged that the lack of treatment would be detrimental to her mental health, and that there is discrimination against persons with a mental health condition in Djibouti.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Dabar argues removal would worsen PTSD, lack of treatment harms mental health, and mental health discrimination exists in Djibouti.

propositions.text: PRRA officer reasonably rejected submissions due to unclear PTSD symptom origin and lack of proof of abuses.
propositions.quote: In my view, the PRRA officer reasonably rejected these submissions. First, as the allegations of political persecution were found not credible, it is unclear what the source of Ms. Dabar’s symptoms is.

propositions.text: Officer reasonably gave little weight to psychotherapist’s fear assertion and found insufficient evidence abuses occurred.
propositions.quote: While the officer accepted the psychotherapist’s statement that Ms. Dabar has symptoms consistent with PTSD, the origin of these symptoms has not been proved. Thus, it was reasonable to give little weight to the psychotherapist’s assertion that Ms. Dabar is “fearful of having to return to Djibouti due to her previous association with the opposition and the possible consequences.” It was equally reasonable for the officer to conclude that “[a]s for returning to the place where she suffered abuses, as previously demonstrated, I find there is insufficient evidence to establish such abuses occurred.”

paragraphs.summary: Court finds officer reasonably rejected submissions due to unclear PTSD origin and insufficient evidence of abuses.

propositions.text: Ms. Dabar argues officer cannot disregard psychotherapist’s factual basis without a hearing and implied credibility finding.
propositions.quote: In this connection, Ms. Dabar argued that the PRRA officer could not disregard the “factual basis” of the psychotherapist’s report without making an implied credibility finding, which cannot be done unless a hearing is held.

propositions.text: I disagree; prior negative credibility findings stand and cannot be overcome by psychotherapist report repeating discredited story.
propositions.quote: I disagree. As she does not challenge the PRRA officer’s findings regarding ethnicity and, most importantly, political persecution, I must assume that the events she alleged did not take place. A PRRA applicant cannot overcome a previous negative credibility finding simply by telling the story found not credible to a health professional and have the professional repeat it in their report: Boyce v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 922 at paragraphs 52–62; Tacoa Veljovic v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2023 FC 1069 at paragraph 44.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Dabar argues officer cannot disregard psychotherapist’s facts without hearing; court disagrees citing prior credibility findings and case law.

propositions.text: Officer reasonably concluded removal despite PTSD symptoms does not amount to persecution.
propositions.quote: Second, it was reasonable for the officer to conclude that removing Ms. Dabar to Djibouti in spite of her PTSD symptoms does not amount to persecution.

propositions.text: Ms. Dabar challenges officer’s statement that she could continue treatment via Internet from Djibouti.
propositions.quote: Ms. Dabar takes issue with the officer’s statement that she could continue her psychological treatment through the Internet from Djibouti.

propositions.text: Statement about Internet treatment is problematic but does not affect reasonableness of outcome.
propositions.quote: I agree that this statement is problematic, as it is unclear whether Ms. Dabar will have a sufficiently stable Internet connexion and the financial resources to pay for the treatment once she no longer lives in Canada. Nevertheless, this does not affect the reasonableness of the outcome,

propositions.text: Unavailability of health services is generally not a valid ground for refugee status; section 97 excludes risks from inability to provide adequate health care.
propositions.quote: because the unavailability of health services in a particular country is generally not understood as a valid ground to claim refugee status. Ms. Dabar has not provided any authority supporting the contrary proposition. With respect to risks covered by section 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [the Act], subparagraph 97(1)(b)(iv) explicitly excludes risks flowing from a country’s “inability” to provide adequate health care.

propositions.text: Covarrubias confirms health service unavailability is excluded from refugee risk under section 97.
propositions.quote: See, in this regard, Covarrubias v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2006 FCA 365 at paragraphs 20–41, [2007] 3 FCR 169.

propositions.text: Mental health service availability issues are better addressed under humanitarian and compassionate grounds, not PRRA.
propositions.quote: In this regard, one should not confuse a PRRA and an application for relief on humanitarian and compassionate grounds pursuant to section 25 of the Act. Issues regarding the availability of mental health services are more properly addressed under the latter process.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds officer reasonably concluded removal despite PTSD is not persecution; health service unavailability excluded from refugee risk.

propositions.text: Officer reasonably rejected claim of widespread mental health stigma due to lack of evidence of personal persecution risk.
propositions.quote: Third, the PRRA officer reasonably rejected Ms. Dabar’s argument that “there is widespread social stigma and discrimination surrounding mental health issues in Djibouti”, as she failed to point to any evidence supporting this assertion and showing that she would be personally affected to the point that it would amount to persecution.

paragraphs.summary: Officer reasonably rejected mental health stigma claim for lack of evidence of personal persecution risk.

propositions.text: Ms. Dabar challenges rejection of gender-based persecution allegations.
propositions.quote: Ms. Dabar also challenges the rejection of her allegations of persecution based on gender.

propositions.text: She provided evidence women in Djibouti face various discrimination forms.
propositions.quote: She provided evidence that women in Djibouti are subject to various forms of discrimination.

propositions.text: PRRA officer acknowledged discrimination but found Ms. Dabar operated business and conditions had not worsened.
propositions.quote: The PRRA officer acknowledged that there is discrimination against women, but found that these conditions existed when Ms. Dabar was living in Djibouti and did not prevent her from operating a business. The officer also noted that there was no indication that these conditions had deteriorated since then.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Dabar challenges gender persecution rejection; officer acknowledged discrimination but found no worsening and noted business operation.

propositions.text: Ms. Dabar argues officer’s reasoning is backward-looking, not forward-looking as required by law.
propositions.quote: Ms. Dabar argues that the officer’s reasoning amounts to a backward-looking assessment of risk instead of the forward-looking assessment mandated by sections 96 and 97 of the Act.

propositions.text: I disagree; officer properly relied on past experience to assess future risk under section 96.
propositions.quote: I disagree. The officer was entitled to rely on Ms. Dabar’s past experience to conclude that she would not face the kind of serious, systematic discrimination that rises to the level of persecution in the future.

propositions.text: Ms. Dabar operated business for two years despite gender; no evidence of worsening discrimination.
propositions.quote: She has been able to operate a business for at least two years despite her gender. Thus, given that she did not point to evidence documenting a deterioration of gender discrimination in Djibouti since her departure, Ms. Dabar is unlikely to face gender-based persecution in the future, which is the threshold that she must meet under section 96 of the Act.

propositions.text: Future risk threshold under section 96 requires forward-looking assessment.
propositions.quote: This does not make the assessment backward-looking.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Dabar argues officer’s reasoning is backward-looking; court disagrees, finding proper forward-looking risk assessment under section 96.

propositions.text: Officer found Ms. Dabar could rely on family for assistance despite their poverty.
propositions.quote: It was also reasonable for the PRRA officer to find that Ms. Dabar could rely on her family for assistance when returning to Djibouti.

propositions.text: Ms. Dabar stated family is poor and living with them would be difficult.
propositions.quote: In her statutory declaration in support of her PRRA application, Ms. Dabar stated that she has a sister and two brothers in Djibouti, but added that they are poor and that it would be difficult for her to live with them.

propositions.text: Officer reasonably found family could provide transitional assistance.
propositions.quote: Given this, it was not unreasonable for the PRRA officer to find that her family would at least be able to provide transitional assistance.

paragraphs.summary: Officer reasonably found Ms. Dabar could rely on family for transitional assistance despite their poverty.

propositions.text: Ms. Dabar argues officer’s finding that she operated business contradicts evidence of forced store closure.
propositions.quote: In her written submissions, Ms. Dabar argues that the PRRA officer’s finding that she could operate a business in Djibouti was contrary to the evidence, because she was forced to close down her store.

propositions.text: I must assume events of forced closure did not occur due to prior credibility findings.
propositions.quote: However, as I explained earlier, I must proceed on the basis that these events did not take place.

propositions.text: RPD found she operated business until March 2017 and it was not shut down by government.
propositions.quote: While Ms. Dabar claimed that the government forcibly closed her store in October 2016, the RPD found that she operated her business until March 2017 and, as a result, that it was not shut down by the government.

propositions.text: Ms. Dabar has not persuaded me that officer’s finding is unreasonable.
propositions.quote: Given these findings, Ms. Dabar has not persuaded me that the PRRA officer’s finding is unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Dabar argues forced store closure contradicts officer’s finding; court assumes closure did not occur and finds officer’s finding reasonable.

propositions.text: Ms. Dabar challenges specific statements about short stay in Somaliland and current support in Canada.
propositions.quote: Ms. Dabar also challenges specific statements in the PRRA decision concerning a short stay in Somaliland and the manner in which she presently supports herself in Canada.

propositions.text: Statements may be incorrect but do not affect officer’s analysis of persecution grounds.
propositions.quote: While these statements may be incorrect, they do not appear to play any role in the officer’s analysis of Ms. Dabar’s four asserted grounds of persecution, in a subsequent part of their reasons.

propositions.text: I am not persuaded these statements play a determinative role in the officer’s reasoning.
propositions.quote: I am not persuaded that they play any determinative role in the PRRA officer’s reasoning.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Dabar challenges some factual statements; court finds they do not affect officer’s persecution analysis or reasoning.

propositions.text: PRRA officer’s decision was reasonable; Ms. Dabar’s judicial review application is dismissed.
propositions.quote: For these reasons, the PRRA officer’s decision was reasonable. Accordingly, Ms. Dabar’s application for judicial review will be dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes PRRA officer’s decision was reasonable and dismisses Ms. Dabar’s judicial review application.
